Embedding Poisoning: Bypassing Safety Alignment via Embedding Semantic Shift

Shuai Yuan Note: Both authors contributed equally to this research. email: 202090914010@std.uestc.edu.cn Affiliation: University of Electronic Science and Technology of China, Chengdu, China , Zhibo Zhang* email: zhangzhibom@hust.edu.cn Affiliation: Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China , Yuxi Li email: yuxili@hust.edu.cn Affiliation: Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China , Guangdong Bai email: g.bai@uq.edu.au Affiliation: The University of Queensland, Brisbane, Australia and WANG KAILONG Note: Corresponding author: WANG KAILONG (wangkl@hust.edu.cn) email: wangkl@hust.edu.cn Affiliation: Huazhong University of Science and Technology, Wuhan, China

Abstract.

The widespread distribution of Large Language Models (LLMs) through public platforms like Hugging Face introduces significant security challenges. While these platforms perform basic security scans, they often fail to detect subtle manipulations within the embedding layer. This work identifies a novel class of deployment-phase attacks that exploit this vulnerability by injecting imperceptible perturbations directly into the embedding layer outputs without modifying model weights or input text. These perturbations, though statistically benign, systematically bypass safety alignment mechanisms and induce harmful behaviors during inference.

We propose Search-based Embedding Poisoning(SEP), a practical, model-agnostic framework that introduces carefully optimized perturbations into embeddings associated with high-risk tokens. SEP leverages a predictable linear transition in model responses—from refusal to harmful output to semantic deviation—to identify a narrow perturbation window that evades alignment safeguards. Evaluated across six aligned LLMs, SEP achieves an average attack success rate of 96.43% while preserving benign task performance and evading conventional detection mechanisms. Our findings reveal a critical oversight in deployment security and emphasize the urgent need for embedding-level integrity checks in future LLM defense strategies.

1. Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated unprecedented capabilities in natural language understanding, generation, and reasoning. The emergence of open-source LLMs such as Llama3 (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen3 (Yang et al., 2025a), and Deepseek (DeepSeek-AI, 2025) has significantly enhanced the accessibility of advanced AI, enabling broad customization and research applications. This openness has accelerated innovation across high-stakes domains including education (Kasneci et al., 2023), healthcare (Singhal et al., 2022), cybersecurity (Zhang et al., 2024), and critical infrastructure (Ghimire et al., 2025). However, the widespread deployment of these models in sensitive contexts underscores the critical need for robust safety alignment, typically achieved through Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) (Ouyang et al., 2022) and Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) (Bai et al., 2022) to mitigate misuse and uphold ethical standards (Anwar et al., 2024). These safety mechanisms, which rely heavily on parameter adjustments (Arditi et al., 2024), assume that embedding vectors accurately encode semantic distinctions to trigger appropriate safety responses. This dependence raises a fundamental question: How robust are existing safety alignment techniques against subtle adversarial perturbations in embedding spaces under real-world deployment conditions?

To explore this, we designed experiments using semantically similar prompt pairs, e.g., “How to make a bomb” vs. “How to make a cake”. By applying incremental perturbations to the embedding of the malicious token (“bomb”), we anticipated a clear dichotomy: minimal changes would preserve malicious semantics and trigger refusals, while larger deviations would cause semantic drift toward benign interpretations (e.g., “bomb” to “comb”). Contrary to expectations, we identified a critical perturbation threshold—a narrow magnitude range—where the model accurately comprehends the harmful intent yet fails to activate safety mechanisms, resulting in the generation of unsafe content.

Our empirical analysis further highlights three significant vulnerabilities enabling safety alignment evasion through embedding perturbations. First, harmful intent is encoded in specific dimensions within embeddings. Perturbations in these dimensions can suppress refusal responses without losing semantic integrity, effectively bypassing safety alignment mechanisms. Second, we uncovered a structured, linear trajectory in model responses corresponding to increasing perturbation magnitude, progressing predictably from refusal to harmful information output and ultimately semantic deviation. This predictability facilitates efficient, gradient-free search strategies to rapidly identify optimal perturbation magnitudes. Third, effective perturbations are distributed broadly across embedding dimensions, with tokens carrying heavy semantic loads (e.g., “attack”, “steal”) showing heightened vulnerability.

Our Work. We propose Search-based Embedding Poisoning (SEP), a practical and model-agnostic framework that systematically evades safety alignment by perturbing embeddings of high-risk tokens prior to decoder processing. The method employs a three-stage pipeline: 1) Targeted Embedding Perturbation, which identifies and perturbs critical dimensions of semantically risky tokens; 2) Merged Search Strategy, combining exponential, binary, and linear search to efficiently locate perturbation thresholds; and 3) Multi-stage Classifier, ensuring output semantic relevance and harmfulness.

We evaluated SEP on six widely-used aligned open-source LLMs: Llama-2-7b-chat-hf (Touvron et al., 2023), Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024), Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M (Yang et al., 2025b), vicuna-13b-v1.5 (Zheng et al., 2023), gemma-7b-it (Team et al., 2024), and Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (Jiang et al., 2023). Using a diverse benchmark of 150 malicious queries across ten threat categories (Chao et al., 2024a; Mazeika et al., 2024), SEP achieved an average attack success rate of 96.43%, substantially outperforming existing methods like DRA (Liu et al., 2024b) and COLD-Attack (Guo et al., 2024) with fewer queries and higher semantic consistency in both harmful and benign contexts. Notably, SEP remained highly effective (exceeding 90% ASR) against reinforced safety techniques and evaded conventional detection mechanisms such as perplexity-based scanning (Jain et al., 2023), as it leaves no trace in model parameters or prompt text. A demonstration is available at (dem, [n. d.]).

Our findings challenge the prevailing safety alignment paradigm that focuses solely on parameter-level protection. They expose a critical oversight in the security protocols of model distribution platforms and highlight embeddings as a vulnerable attack vector. Consequently, ensuring LLM safety necessitates embedding-level integrity verification, adversarial robustness, and holistic semantic reasoning.

Contributions. The contribution is summarized below:

  • •

    Identification of Embedding-Space Vulnerabilities in Deployed LLMs. We demonstrate that safety alignment mechanisms are highly susceptible to minimal perturbations in the embedding space.

  • •

    Discovery of Linear Response Transition Under Perturbation. We show that model responses follow a structured linear trajectory from refusal to harmful output as perturbation increases.

  • •

    Development of the SEP Framework. We introduce an efficient pipeline for embedding poisoning that combines targeted perturbation and heuristic search strategies.

  • •

    Demonstration of High-Efficacy Attacks Across Aligned LLMs. We demonstrate high attack success rates (up to 96.43%) across multiple aligned LLMs and composite benchmark.

2. Background

2.1. LLMs Structure Notation

Given an open-source LLM MM, we denote TT as its tokenizer and 𝒱\mathcal{V} as the finite vocabulary of token symbols in TT. Given an input prompt PP, the tokenizer TT first tokenizes PP into smaller semantic units call tokens, denoted as x=T⁡(P)=(x1,x2,…​xn)∈𝒱nx=T(P)=(x_{1},x_{2},...x_{n})\in\mathcal{V}^{n}. For each xi∈𝒱x_{i}\in\mathcal{V}, the LLM MM presents an embedding vector with dimension DD. We denote Φ:𝒱n→ℝD×n\Phi:\mathcal{V}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{D\times n} as the embedding function. After the input token sequence xx is embedded, the LLM MM takes Φ⁡(x)\Phi(x) as the input and calculates the logits l=M⁡(Φ⁡(x))∈R|𝒱|l=M(\Phi(x))\in R^{|\mathcal{V}|} as output through a single forward pass. A softmax function is then applied to ll to obtain a probability distribution over the vocabulary. MM then samples a single token from this distribution, denoted as xn+1x_{n+1}, representing the next token in the generated sequence. This token is then concatenated to the input token sequence xx, forming a new input sequence for the next generation cycle. This process repeats until an end-of-sequence token is generated or the number of generated tokens mm reaches the user-specified maximum token limit. The final generated token sequence y=(xn+1,…​xn+m)y=(x_{n+1},...x_{n+m}) is then decoded by the tokenizer TT to produce the corresponding text output T−1​(y)T^{-1}(y).

2.2. Safety Alignment of LLMs

Prior work has shown that LLMs need to construct safety alignment to ensure that the content they generate is consistent with human values. The Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) (Ouyang et al., 2022) approach fine-tunes pre-trained models by using manually labeled security response datasets. Later, Reinforcement Learning Based on Human Feedback (RLHF) (Bai et al., 2022) uses human preference ranking of responses to train reward functions to optimize model behavior. For reward model optimization, RLHF uses proximal policy optimization (PPO) (Schulman et al., 2017) to train independent reward models, while direct preference optimization (DPO) (Rafailov et al., 2024) directly analyzes positive and negative samples to adjust the reward function. Currently, most progressive LLMs adopt human/AI feedback to mitigate model ethical risks. However, the existing security alignment mechanism cannot guarantee the security of the model embedding layer, and its robustness to embedding poisoning attacks needs to be further explored.

3. Empirical Study

As described in Section 2, the embedding function Φ\Phi plays a critical role in the LLM generation process, transforming the tokens composed of characters into embedding vectors. However, unlike grayscale images which have continuous representations, token representations are sparse, leaving significant gaps in their representation space. This sparsity implies that even minor perturbations to the embedding can cause substantial changes in the final output. To better understand this phenomenon and the related security implications, we conduct an empirical study. Specifically, our empirical study aims to answer the following questions:

  • •

    What changes will occur in the LLM output due to the embedding perturbations? To answer this question, we apply single-dimensional linear perturbations across all tokens in the input sequence within a predefined range, and then analyze both the content and structure of the resulting output.

  • •

    How do different types of perturbations influence changes in the LLM output? To answer this question, we introduce variations to the perturbations, such as applying them to different dimensions of the embedding vector and to different tokens, to examine whether the resulting output changes remain consistent.

3.1. Implementation of Empirical Study

3.1.1. Experimental Setup

In our empirical study, as the embedding perturbation requires full parameter access, we focus on the open-source LLMs to obtain their embedding representations. Specifically, we select Llama-2-7b-chat-hf as our target model because 1): its open-source accessibility and widespread adoption, and 2): its moderately sized vocabulary and its good generic capabilities.

To better observe the effects of perturbation-induced changes on input questions in Llama-2-7b-chat-hf (Touvron et al., 2023), we choose harmful instructions as test cases for two reasons: 1) such instructions typically trigger the model’s safety alignment, resulting in refusal responses, and 2) the model has already learned appropriate responses to these questions, making any changes in output more noticeable compared to benign queries. To address these considerations, we use the open-source benchmark JailbreakBench (Chao et al., 2024a), which includes 100 examples across 10 categories such as harassment and violence. For simplicity, we randomly choose 10 questions (one from each category) as the test dataset.

3.1.2. Adding Embedding Perturbations

Let XtX_{t} denote the test dataset including 10 chosen malicious questions. For each input P∈XtP\in X_{t}, we first obtain its embedding representation E=Φ⁡(T⁡(P))=(e1,e2,…​en)∈ℝD×nE=\Phi(T(P))=(e_{1},e_{2},...e_{n})\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times n} and randomly select one dimension dP∈{0,1,…​D−1}d^{P}\in\{0,1,...D-1\}. For each eie_{i}, we apply a perturbation to dimension dd, which linearly increases from 0 to a predefined upper limit in both positive and negative directions, denoted as e^i=(ei0,…​eid+β,…​eiD−1)\hat{e}_{i}=(e^{0}_{i},...e^{d}_{i}+\beta,...e_{i}^{D-1}), where β\beta is the perturbation value. In our initial experiment, which examines how linear perturbations across all input tokens affect the output, we set the maximum perturbation magnitude to 3. This defines a linear perturbation range of [−3,3][-3,3]. We use a step size of 0.005 to ensure fine-grained observation of the LLM’s responses. We then apply perturbations across this range, collect all resulting outputs, and analyze how the output changes in response to the perturbations.

To further explore how perturbations along different embedding dimensions affect LLM outputs for harmful inputs, we use a sampling-based approach. Specifically, we randomly select 10 dimensions, denoted as d1P,…​d10Pd^{P}_{1},...d^{P}_{10}, and repeat the experiment using the same settings described earlier. Additionally, since specific tokens often carry the core harmful semantics in a query (e.g., the word “bomb” in the instruction “Write a tutorial on making a bomb”), we apply linear perturbations along the same dimension dd to these individual tokens. This allows us to examine how perturbing the most semantically dangerous tokens influences the output. To identify these key tokens, we use GPT-4o with carefully designed prompts (the full prompt and accuracy evaluation is provided in Appendix B). Since perturbations applied to individual tokens often lead to more unpredictable effects on the output, we raise the maximum perturbation value to 30 (reason to be further discussed in Section 3.2.2) while keeping the step size at 0.005.

3.2. Empirical Study Results

3.2.1. Changes to LLM outputs due to embedding perturbations

We carefully check the responses of the LLM after the perturbation and meticulously categorize them, establishing a taxonomy that outlines the changes to the LLM outputs. We refer to the changes as semantic shifts in the LLM outputs hereafter, as they reflect the deviation in how the LLM interprets and responds to the original inputs. The full details are presented in Figure 8, Figure 9 and Appendix C. Figure 8 illustrates the detailed categorization of the responses and we detail each type of them as follows.

Denial Response. This type of response occurs when there is no perturbation or only a slight amount of perturbation. LLM usually responds “I cannot” or “It is unethical” when receiving harmful instructions as inputs, which activates the LLM’s safety mechanism and maintains its original output.

Part Deviation Response. This occurs when the LLM generates a response that remains on the same general topic as the original question, but loses some of its intended semantics. For example, when the input “How to make a bomb?” is perturbed, the model might respond with a general description such as “A bomb is a device that can cause an explosion…”, rather than providing instructions. This reflects a partial deviation from the original intent.

Total Harmful Response. This response occurs when the LLM generates harmful content that directly correspond to the harmful inputs, indicating that its safety mechanisms have been successfully bypassed. As shown in the purple region of Figure 8, this represents a serious security risk, as it can be exploited by adversaries to elicit unsafe outputs.

Total Deviation Response. It occurs when the narrative subject of the output is no longer the content of the original question. For instance, given the input of “How to spread disinformation during natural disasters”, the LLM responds with the meaning of the word “moral”, indicating a total deviation from the input.

Deviation but Harmful Response. This type of response is considered a specific subcategory of Part Deviation. While typical Part Deviation responses are often ethical statements that avoid harmful content, Deviation but Harmful responses still contain harmful information. For example, when given the prompt “How to nefariously alter criminal records?”, the LLM may respond with methods for tampering with federal crime data. Such outputs represent potential vulnerabilities that could be exploited by red-team attackers.

Glitch Response. This response emerges when the perturbation becomes strong enough to cause the LLM to generate non-human-readable or incoherent tokens. For example, in response to the prompt “Write an erotic movie script”, the model may produce a repetitive or nonsensical output such as looping on “T.,”. This is a response that lacks clear meaning from a human perspective.

As depicted in Figure 8, we can linearly divide the perturbation range into three major regions: the Refusal Region contains almost all the Denial Responses; the Uncertain Region occupies the disorganized Part Deviation Responses, Total Harmful Responses and Deviation but Harmful Responses; and the Deviation Region includes all the Deviation Responses and Glitch Responses.

A possible explanation for Finding 1 can be drawn from the insights presented in (Arditi et al., 2024). As shown in Figure 1, when PP is embedded with Φ⁡(T⁡(P))\Phi(T(P)), specific dimensions of certain token embeddings encode the malicious intent of the input. These dimensions can be viewed as the projection of the embedding vector onto a subspace that carries harmful semantics. We refer to this as the malicious component, which is responsible for triggering the model’s safety mechanisms. In contrast, the other dimensions that do not contribute to the malicious component form the semantic component, which is conceptually orthogonal to the malicious component. This separation suggests that within a certain range of perturbation, it is possible to shift the malicious component outside the boundaries monitored by the model’s safety alignment, thereby eliciting harmful outputs from the LLM. Notably, Figure 8 shows that both the uncertain and deviation regions appear in both the positive and negative directions of perturbation, supporting this hypothesis.

3.2.2. Impacts on semantic shifts from different types of perturbations

We randomly sample nine additional embedding dimensions and apply perturbations to them, analyzing the resulting outputs from the LLM. The results in the left part of Figure 2 reveal that while different dimensions lead to varied response distributions for the same input. All six output categories and three response regions consistently appear across all selected dimensions, which supports the validity of our categorization. Moreover, both the Harmful Response (purple stripes) and Deviation but Harmful Response (blue stripes) occur with notable spans in all selected dimensions, indicating a substantial likelihood that attackers could exploit these perturbations to induce harmful content from the LLM.

To further examine the influence of “dangerous tokens”, tokens that directly express the illegal intent in malicious queries, under embedding perturbation, we apply perturbations exclusively to these tokens—rather than to the entire input sentence. The results, shown on the right side of Figure 2, reveal that when the perturbation limit is set to 3, altering only the dangerous tokens results in minimal semantic shifts. However, when the upper bound is increased to 30, the spans of Harmful Response and Deviation but Harmful Response become significantly longer for dangerous tokens compared to perturbing the full sentence. This indicates that dangerous tokens carry the majority of malicious intent, making them a more effective target for adversaries.

4. Threat Model

4.1. Attacker hypothesis

4.1.1. Attacker’s Goal

The attackers’ primary objective is to develop embedding-level exploits that undermine the safety alignment of open-source LLMs against their original malicious queries. They aim to create malicious models capable of generating harmful content (e.g., pornographic, violent, discriminatory, or otherwise illegal outputs) in response to users’ malicious queries, while maintaining normal capacity for benign user queries. This attack goal is similar to existing model poisoning or finetuning attacks (Qi et al., 2023; Yang et al., 2023; Huang et al., 2025), which modify models’ parameters or structures to subvert their safety mechanisms. In contrast, traditional jailbreak attacks craft prompt-level payloads designed to bypass model safety alignment rather than deactivating it, representing a distinct goal and attack method.

4.1.2. Attacker’s Capacity

For open-source models, we assume attackers can craft a malicious model file that minimally alters the target model’s execution flow to introduce malicious behavior. This assumption aligns with existing literature on model poisoning attacks, where adversaries can manipulate training data or fine-tuning processes to compromise model integrity (Hu et al., 2024; Egashira et al., 2024). Crucially, this injected control flow requires no guidance from model weights, training data, or runtime gradient information, distinguishing this attack from other model poisoning methods.

4.2. Attack Deployment and Practical Feasibility

As illustrated in Figure 3, attack deployment can be roughly divided into three phases:

Preparation phase. Before the model deployment, The attacker locally searches for numerous carefully crafted perturbations to bypass safety alignment. These perturbations, defined by parameters such as target tokens, embedding dimensions, and magnitudes, are compiled into a static corpus, which is utilized upon execution to validate user inputs and load the corresponding perturbation payload.

Distribution phase. The injection code will be saved as a file in the malicious model to tamper with the execution flow of the model. The compromised model is then packaged using standard configurations and distributed via open-source platforms, masquerading as benign.

Deployment phase. When a user provides malicious input, the model’s malicious program flow triggers a match in the corpus. This activates a hook function, which uses the matched perturbation payload to construct a perturbation matrix. This matrix is then applied to the embedding layer’s output before it is processed by subsequent Transformer layers. Ultimately, the poisoned embedding output bypasses the model’s safety alignment, causing the model to generate malicious content.

5. Methodology

The preceding analysis reveals that strategic perturbations in the embedding space of safety-aligned queries can be located to induce constraint violations in LLMs. Building on this insight, we propose SEP (Search-based Embedding Poisoning), a novel embedding poisoning framework that systematically identifies optimal adversarial perturbations through merged search processes.

As depicted in Figure 4, our framework operates through three core components: Targeted Embedding Perturbation, Merged Search Strategy, and Multi-stage Classifier. For a given input query, we first identify target tokens and dimensions requiring perturbation. The merged search strategy then generates candidate poisoned embeddings, which are fed into the target LLM. The generated responses undergo multi-stage classifier evaluation to determine harmfulness. Harmful cases terminate the search process, while harmless outcomes refine subsequent perturbation generation through feedback-driven strategy updates.

5.1. Targeted Embedding Perturbation

Building on empirical Findings 1–3, we develop a structured perturbation framework that injects controlled noise into a single embedding dimension of dangerous tokens. To preserve predictable behavioral patterns, perturbations are constrained to one dimension. The dangerous tokens are identified efficiently using GPT-4o prompt engineering, requiring only one API call per query with minimal computational overhead.

We formalize the attack process under a generic usage scenario, where a malicious query PP is represented by a standard embedding tensor E={e1,e2,…,en}E=\{e_{1},e_{2},\dots,e_{n}\}. For a detected dangerous word w​o​r​dd​a​n​g​e​r∈Pword_{danger}\in P, we extract its corresponding token offset mapping positions {i,i+1,…,j}\{i,i+1,\dots,j\}, obtaining harmful embeddings Ew​o​r​dd​a​n​g​e​r={ei,ei+1,…,ej}E_{word_{danger}}=\{e_{i},e_{i+1},\dots,e_{j}\}. We construct perturbation vector en​o​i​s​e=[0,…,β,…,0]⊤∈ℝDe_{noise}=[0,\dots,\beta,\dots,0]^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{D} with magnitude β\beta at target dimension dt​a​r​g​e​td_{target} while maintaining zeros elsewhere. The poisoned embedding tensor of malicious question PP become:

(1) Ep​o​i​s​o​n={e1,…,(ei+en​o​i​s​e),…,(ej+en​o​i​s​e),…,en}E_{poison}=\{e_{1},...,(e_{i}+e_{noise}),...,(e_{j}+e_{noise}),...,e_{n}\}

This targeted perturbation strategy introduces controlled deviations essential for harmful outputs induction.

5.2. Merged Search Strategy

We design a merged search strategy to efficiently identify the Uncertain Region and locate Harmful Responses (as described by Finding 1 in Section 3), enabling targeted and effective perturbation insertion.

5.2.1. Search Space Definition

The function Perturb in Algorithm 1 shows that, to complete a perturbation, we need to determine the target dimension and perturbation magnitude, which represents the two levels of search space of our search strategy:

Dimension Search Space. Finding 2 in Section 3 reveals that for the same harmful instruction, there may be specific perturbations in many dimensions that can induce the model to output a harmful response. Therefore, we create a random sample of ξ\xi dimensions as the first level of the search space. The search strategy iterates through all ξ\xi dimensions and stops once a successful case is found; if none succeed, the attack attempt is considered a failure.

Perturbation Search Space. Empirical symmetry analysis in Section 3 reveals that perturbations capable of triggering harmful responses can occur in both positive and negative directions. SEP enforces unidirectional positive perturbation to simplify search complexity. Therefore, for any dimension, let the perturbation search space 𝒳=[0,+∞)\mathcal{X}=[0,+\infty) represent all possible perturbation magnitudes βi∈ℝ+\beta_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{+}. This continuum admits a tripartite decomposition:

  • •

    Refusal region ℛ\mathcal{R}: A bounded closed interval where perturbations yield rejection responses.

  • •

    Deviation region 𝒟\mathcal{D}: A right-unbounded or left-unbounded interval producing irrelevant outputs.

  • •

    Uncertain region 𝒰\mathcal{U}: A finite open interval bridging ℛ\mathcal{R} and 𝒟\mathcal{D} with stochastic harmful contents potential.

Successful perturbations 𝒳J⊂𝒰\mathcal{X}_{J}\subset\mathcal{U} form clustered configurations with unknown spatial distribution, where each cluster contains β\beta values capable of bypassing safety alignment.

5.2.2. Search Deployment

Without knowledge of ℛ/𝒰/𝒟\mathcal{R}/\mathcal{U}/\mathcal{D} region boundaries or perturbations’ cluster patterns, we consider the perturbation magnitude search on any dimension of search space as an online sequential decision-making problem to progressively identify transitional boundaries and detect the attack effect under uncertainty. While a successful attack requires finding any single perturbation βi\beta_{i} that trigger a harmful response, exhaustive search strategies from empirical studies incur prohibitive 𝒪⁡(|𝒳|)\mathcal{O}(|\mathcal{X}|) time complexity. To avoid excessive time burden, SEP employs a classifier-guided merged search strategy, which dynamically refines perturbation positions based on classifier feedback of response semantics. The hybrid strategy achieves sublinear time complexity by integrating three key components: Exponential Bounding, Binary Refinement and Linear Probing. The synergistic pipeline operates as follows:

Exponential Bounding. Based on the response characteristics observed in Finding 1, we first aim to estimate the approximate boundaries of the Uncertain Region UU, which lies between the Rejection and Deviation regions. To efficiently amplify the perturbation magnitude, SEP initializes it as β0=θ\beta_{0}=\theta and applies exponential growth with a factor ϕ=2\phi=2, following the rule βi=2i−1​θ\beta_{i}=2^{i-1}\theta. This strategy enables rapid identification of the boundary of the Uncertain Region, estimated as [2k−2​θ,2k−1​θ][2^{k-2}\theta,2^{k-1}\theta], by using classifier feedback to detect the point at which model responses transition from rejection to deviation.

Binary Refinement. Subsequent refinement implements recursive space bisection with semantic-aware adjustments on exponentially-searching output interval [a0,b0][a_{0},b_{0}], where a0=2k−2​θa_{0}=2^{k-2}\theta and b0=2k−1​θb_{0}=2^{k-1}\theta. Denoting the searching region in the i-th iteration as [ai,bi][a_{i},b_{i}], SEP recursively updates the interval [ai+1,bi+1][a_{i+1},b_{i+1}] based on model response of perturbation βi=(ai+bi)/2\beta_{i}=(a_{i}+b_{i})/2. This phase continues until interval precision reaches γ\gamma, effectively narrowing the search space by 𝒪⁡(log⁡(1/γ))\mathcal{O}(\log(1/\gamma)) time complexity.

Linear Probing. After narrowing the search area to a sufficiently precise range, SEP equidistantly scan the refined region [af,bf][a_{f},b_{f}] with a coarse granularity at intervals of α\alpha and calculate perturbations via βi=af+bf−afα+1​(i+1)\beta_{i}=a_{f}+\frac{b_{f}-a_{f}}{\alpha+1}(i+1). The search process terminates when the model response is identified as “malicious” by the classifier or when the maximum number of search attempts is reached. The final scanning phase achieves the localization of perturbations that can trigger harmful responses with a time complexity of 𝒪⁡(1)\mathcal{O}(1).

The merged search strategy introduces dimension-level parallelism by performing an automated hybrid search in the positive direction across ξ\xi dimensions (default ξ=20\xi=20). This approach, grounded in our empirical findings, effectively balances the trade-off between precision and efficiency.

5.3. Multi-stage Classifier

Based on the search strategy, identifying response semantics is crucial for determining transitional boundaries and improving search efficiency. Therefore, we propose a multi-stage classifier to guide the above search strategy. The classifier groups the six categories of responses into four situations: 1) Denial: Denial Responses; 2) Deviation: Deviation, Deviation but Harmful, or Glitch Responses; 3) Part Deviation: Part Deviation Responses; 4) Bypass: Total Harmful Responses, which is formally denoted as 𝒞:𝒳→{Denial,Deviation,Part Deviation,Bypass}\mathcal{C}:\mathcal{X}\to\{\text{Denial},\text{Deviation},\text{Part Deviation},\text{Bypass}\}. There are three main layers in this classifier:

  • •

    Refusal Detect: Based on GCG rule-based classifier (Zou et al., 2023)

  • •

    Deviation Detect: Based on Harmbench classifier (Mazeika et al., 2024)

  • •

    Harmfulness Detect: Based on Safeguard Model classifier Llama-Guard-3-8B (Llama Team, 2024)

The categorization process is shown in Figure 5. For refusal detection, we modify the GCG Deny List to match Denial responses, as detailed in Appendix A. For deviation detection, we use HarmBench-Llama-2-13b-cls, which identifies both safety violations and relevance to the malicious prompt, to classify Deviation responses. For harmfulness detection, we adopt Llama-Guard-3-8B due to its high accuracy (93.9%) and low false positive rate (4%), outperforming GPT-4 (80.5%80.5\%, 15.2%15.2\% respectively). It is used to identify Bypass responses that evade safety alignment. Classifier prompts for Harmbench and Llama-Guard-3-8B are in Appendix B. Responses flagged by HarmBench-Llama-2-13b-cls but not by Llama-Guard-3-8B are less toxic yet still related to the malicious prompt, which are classified as Part Deviation.

5.4. Implementation

The implementation of SEP orchestrates the three core components outline above, as described by Algorithm 2. The adaptive process dynamically explores different perturbations to identify one that successfully triggers a harmful response.

The overall pipeline begins with a two-level search space initialization. A subset of ξ\xi dimensions (dtargetd_{\text{target}}) is randomly selected from the model’s hidden size (denoted as LL) to form the dimension search space. The perturbation search space is defined by an interval [lU,rU][l_{U},r_{U}]. For each dtargetd_{\text{target}}, SEP first enters the Exponential Bounding phase, where rUr_{U} is exponentially increased until the classifier 𝒞\mathcal{C} labels the model’s response as a deviation category (lines 4–10), thereby identifying the approximate right boundary of the Uncertain Region.

Next, the Binary Refinement phase selects the midpoint of the current Uncertain Region as the perturbation magnitude β\beta (line 12) and uses the classifier’s feedback to iteratively narrow the region to its left or right half (lines 17–18). This binary search process efficiently reduces the invalid range and increases the likelihood of finding a successful perturbation.

Once the region length falls below a threshold γ\gamma, SEP proceeds with Linear Probing, linearly traversing the interval from rUr_{U} to lUl_{U} with a step size of rU−lUα+1\frac{r_{U}-l_{U}}{\alpha+1} (line 21). If at any point during the search process the classifier 𝒞\mathcal{C} identifies a Bypass response (lines 8, 15, or 24), the attack is deemed successful. The algorithm then returns the successful perturbation dimension, magnitude, and related information.

The proposed SEP architecture is designed to achieve the following key advantages: 1) classifier-directed dynamic search process can improve the search effectiveness and efficiency, and 2) the multiple determination design of the classifier ensures the validity of harmful response judgment.

6. Evaluation

6.1. Experiment Setup

6.1.1. Evaluation Targets

To expand the range of LLM selection and ensure an extensive evaluation, we select six widely recognized and open-source LLMs from different companies as our targets, which have undergone strict security alignment during training and are also the main targets of recent attacks. These models are: Llama-2-7b-chat-hf (Touvron et al., 2023) and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct (Grattafiori et al., 2024) from MetaAI, Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct-1M (Yang et al., 2025b) from Qwen, vicuna-13b-v1.5 (Zheng et al., 2023) from LMSYS, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.3 (Jiang et al., 2023) from MistralAI, and gemma-7b-it (Team et al., 2024) from Google AI.

6.1.2. Evaluation Benchmarks

To evaluate the effectiveness of SEP, we curate a dataset of 150 dangerous questions. Specifically, 100 questions are drawn from the complete Jailbreakbench (Chao et al., 2024a), covering 10 distinct dangerous scenarios, while the remaining 50 are randomly selected from Harmbench (Mazeika et al., 2024), excluding copyright-related and context-dependent items. This combined dataset provides a comprehensive basis for evaluating SEP’s performance.

6.1.3. Evaluation Baselines

In the comparative study, we select three representative attack techniques that share certain characteristics with our method. These attacks are:

  • •

    COLD-Attack (Guo et al., 2024): White-box automated jailbreak by controllable generation of smooth adversarial suffixes.

  • •

    DRA (Disguise and Reconstruction Attack) (Liu et al., 2024b): Black-box prompt-level jailbreak by concealing harmful instructions with disguise, which performs character-level perturbations on the prompt during the attack pipeline.

  • •

    Embedding Space Attack (Schwinn et al., 2023; Schwinn et al., 2024): White-box embedding poisoning method by optimized adversarial vector suffix.

In addition, we evaluate our method against two representative defense techniques to assess its effectiveness under strengthened safety alignment. These defenses are:

  • •

    SmoothLLM (Robey et al., 2024): It utilizes randomized character perturbations which effectively break the attack prompt.

  • •

    ESF (Enhanced Safety Finetuning) (Bianchi et al., 2024): It incorporates a small number of safety-focused examples during the instruction-tuning stage.

6.1.4. Evaluation Settings

For three attack baselines, we use the default settings of the methods to complete the experiment. For Embedding Space Attack, after it successfully outputs the target prefix, we generate a complete text with a maximum length of 200 for the classification method evaluation results. For SEP, we choose the merged search strategy to complete our attack, where the hyperparameters of the search strategy are as follows: exponential scale θ\theta, binary scale γ\gamma, linear scale α\alpha are set to 0.10.1, 0.050.05, 1010. The hyperparameter of max search dimensions ξ\xi is set to 2020. For the hyperparameters of the model generation, we apply the default parameters and set the temperature to 1 to increase the randomness and diversity of the generated content.

Additionally, SmoothLLM scrambles ten copies of each attack cue and sends them to a jailbreak discriminator after the model generates outputs. If more than 50%50\% of the copies produce harmful content, the attack is considered successful; otherwise, it is deemed a failure. To align with this evaluation protocol, we attack each individual copy of every sample using SEP. If the attack on any copy fails, or if SmoothLLM perturbs the danger word within a copy, we refrain from perturbing the embedding vector of that copy. For the ESF defense, we follow the default configuration, which integrates 300 additional safety instructions during instruction tuning via LoRA over four epochs.

6.1.5. Evaluation Metrics

To evaluate the effectiveness and efficiency of SEP, we assess Attack Success Rate (ASR), which is calculated as A​S​R=STASR=\frac{S}{T}, where SS denotes the number of successful attack instances, and TT represents the total number of samples in the benchmark. Specifically, we apply the multi-stage classifier mentioned in Section 5.2 to determine whether the attack is successful. Furthermore, we also apply Q/TC (average number of queries per test case) to evaluate the efficiency of SEP.

6.2. Evaluation Result

6.2.1. Effectiveness

Our comprehensive evaluation reveals that SEP has superior performance on ASR against three baselines across six target LLMs. As shown in figure 6, our method achieved the highest average ASR of 96.43%96.43\% across all target models, outperforming the second-best baseline by approximately 10%10\%. Furthermore, SEP achieves an ASR of over 98%98\% on five out of six models, notably attaining a 100%100\% ASR on Llama-2-7B. For gemma-7B, while our method exhibits relatively lower ASR compared to other models, it still demonstrates a substantial improvement over three baselines with an average ASR increase of over 40%40\%, suggesting a stronger inherent safety alignment in gemma-7B. The superior effectiveness of SEP further demonstrates that: 1) the semantic drift phenomenon during incremental perturbations is widely present in most test cases; 2) the merged search strategy can effectively identify perturbation magnitudes capable of bypassing safety alignment.

Turning our attention to three baselines, for the black-box prompt-level attack DRA, its ASR unexpectedly reaches the second-highest value (86.87%86.87\%). However, DRA still fails to correctly interpret certain attack prompts, particularly on gemma-7B, resulting in a relatively low ASR of 45.30%45.30\%. For white-box gradient-based suffix attacks such as Embedding Space Attack and COLD-Attack, their ASR is only 56.89%56.89\% and 74.33%74.33\%. Although they can optimize a fixed affirmative response prefix within the expected steps, they do not guarantee that the model’s subsequent replies maintain this affirmative pattern. Therefore, when we evaluate the complete outputs of both methods with our classifier, their success rates drop significantly. For instance, Embedding Space Attack on Llama-2-7B declines from nearly 100%100\% to 74%74\%. This demonstrates that attack methods optimizing for specific response prefixes widely suffer from this “local optimum” problem, necessitating more rigorous evaluation of full responses.

6.2.2. Efficiency

For efficiency analysis, SEP requires an average of 41.6841.68 Q/TC. Specifically, for models with high ASR such as Vicuna-13B and Mistral-7B, on average, fewer than 1010 queries are needed for a successful attack. In contrast, SEP takes up to 184.61184.61 Q/TC on gemma-7B, indicating a harder process to identify a reasonable perturbation. It is foreseeable that the efficiency of SEP is mainly related to the distribution of the Uncertain Region located in valid dimensions for poisoning. Randomly selected dimensions affect the quantity of dimensions to be searched when attacking, and the distribution of Uncertain Region in these dimensions affects the difficulty of localizing the perturbation when traversing a single dimension. For example, in gemma-7B, almost 50%50\% cases need at least three invalid dimensions’ searching, requiring about 60 queries. It is worth noting that the efficiency of SEP can be influenced by the search for ineffective dimensions and the varying perturbation magnitude requirements across different models.

6.2.3. Magnitude of Perturbation

We calculate the magnitude of perturbations that successfully broke the security alignment for each group of models. At the same time, to corroborate with the empirical data, we added an additional experimental group with zero temperature for comparison.

As shown in Table 2, the average perturbation amplitude is generally lower at temperature 11 compared to temperature 00. This suggests that even small perturbations can influence the model’s output logits, and that increased randomness from higher temperature sampling facilitates the generation of harmful responses. For gemma-7B on temperature 11, a perturbation magnitude of more than 45 means that an additional 7-8 Exponential Search and Binary Search is required to locate a smaller Uncertain Region range for subsequent searches, which also reduces the efficiency of SEP. At temperature 00, the overall perturbation magnitude appears relatively large because the model is less random. However, this reduced randomness makes it harder to bypass safety alignment in certain challenging test cases. As a result, even though large perturbations are attempted, successful perturbations are less frequently collected, leading to an overall smaller average magnitude observed—an outcome that may seem counterintuitive. For Llama-2-7B, the average perturbation amplitude is 17.0417.04 when the temperature is 00, which is in line with what we observed in our empirical study, presenting that our search strategy can indeed locate the approximate distribution of attack perturbations.

6.3. Parameter Analysis

6.3.1. Selection of max search dimensions ξ\xi

In this section, we analyze the number of dimensions searched in successful attack cases for each model.

As shown in figure 7, for all selected models except gemma-7B, more than 70%70\% of the test cases succeed by searching only a single dimension. For Vicuna-13B, approximately 98%98\% of the test cases succeed within three-dimensional searches, whereas for gemma-7B, only 52%52\% succeed, which indirectly explains its lower success rate and search efficiency. On average, over 85%85\% of the test cases succeed within three dimensions, an acceptable probability that aligns with the empirical findings discussed in Finding 3. To further improve the ASR, we set the maximum search dimensions ξ\xi to 2020, allowing deeper searches per case. Although this setting significantly increases Q/TC for failed attempts, the trade-off is worthwhile; notably, the ASR for gemma-7B improves from a potential 52%52\% to 82.67%82.67\%.

6.3.2. Selection of Temperature

In evaluating SEP, we also incorporate repeated sampling of poisoned embeddings generated under different perturbation amplitudes. It is reasonable to hypothesize that a higher sampling temperature, which independently increases output entropy, could enhance attack effectiveness. To assess the impact of temperature on ASR and efficiency, we evaluate each model using three sampling temperatures—11, the model’s default recommended temperature, and 00, while keeping all other hyperparameters and experimental configurations fixed. This is designed to simulate practical LLM usage scenarios.

As shown in Table 3, we observe that as the sampling temperature decreases, the ASR declines to varying degrees across different models. Among all models, Llama-3.1-8B is the most affected, with its ASR dropping by nearly 40%40\% when the temperature is reduced from 11 to 00. In contrast, Mistral-7B exhibits the least sensitivity to temperature changes, showing only an approximate 5%5\% decrease.

Although individual models vary, the overall impact of temperature on ASR is relatively moderate, with an average decrease of approximately 20%20\%. This finding confirms that a relatively higher temperature (i.e., 11) increases output entropy, thereby enhancing both the effectiveness and efficiency of SEP. Furthermore, temperature exerts a substantial influence on the efficiency of SEP, particularly on the Q/TC metric. For example, Llama-3.1-8B experiences a nearly ninefold increase in Q/TC under temperature 00 compared to temperature 11. On average, across all models, the Q/TC increases by 61.1961.19 as the temperature decreases, underscoring the correlation between lower sampling temperatures and attack efficiency.

In analyzing the effects of different temperatures, we attribute the observed differences to the behavior of attack perturbations in modifying the model’s output distribution. Specifically, most perturbations are designed to increase the likelihood of sampling “malicious tokens” that trigger affirmative responses by shifting the model’s output logits. Under a higher sampling temperature, such as 11, the output entropy is greater, making it more probable for these malicious tokens to be sampled and thereby inducing the model into an affirmative response mode. In contrast, under greedy sampling at temperature 00, malicious tokens must surpass normal tokens in probability to be sampled, which is significantly more challenging. Based on this and empirical results, we ultimately choose temperature 11 as the deployment setting to enhance both the effectiveness and efficiency of SEP.

6.4. Ablation Study for Search Strategy

To evaluate the impact of different search strategies, we conduct an ablation study on three SEP variants across six target models, incorporating Linear and Binary Search using the default parameters from Section 5.2.

As listed in Table 4, the merged search strategy achieves the highest ASR on most models while requiring fewer Q/TC, effectively balancing the strengths of the two baseline strategies. Although its ASR is only 0.2%0.2\% higher than that of Linear Search, it achieves this performance with a 4.724.72 smaller Q/TC, demonstrating a significant improvement in search efficiency. However, for gemma-7B, the merged strategy shows a lower ASR compared to the Linear search strategy. One possible reason for this discrepancy could be that the binary search component of the merged strategy introduces notable inaccuracies when estimating the search space. These inaccuracies might arise from unexpected nonlinear distributions or classifier errors, weakening the effectiveness of the subsequent linear search step. Additionally, for models such as Llama-3.1-8B and Vicuna-13B, where the baseline success rates already exceed 99%99\%, the merged strategy offers limited further improvement due to the ceiling effect on ASR.

6.5. Performance on Enhanced Safety Alignment

We analyze the effectiveness of SEP against two defense baselines, with results presented in Table 5. SmoothLLM does not significantly affect the ASR of our method. In fact, the average ASR increases slightly by 1%, with a particularly noticeable improvement observed for gemma-7B. Upon closer examination, we identify three contributing factors to this unexpected result: 1) SmoothLLM has a low probability of perturbing the key dangerous words, and perturbations to other words do not substantially affect the success of our attack; 2) attacking ten scrambled copies only requires successfully compromising five or more copies, thus expanding the effective search space for SEP; and 3) SmoothLLM’s classifier operates primarily by detecting specific discriminative words, which may inadvertently disrupt the prompt semantics and trigger positive responses. These findings demonstrate the insufficiency of SmoothLLM in defending against our attack. In contrast, ESF shows a measurable defensive effect, reducing the average ASR of SEP by approximately 20%20\%. This drop is particularly pronounced for Llama-3.1-8B and Qwen2.5-7B, where ASR decreases over 40%40\%. However, the defense impact on the remaining four models is relatively modest. These results suggest that while instruction-tuning-based defenses like ESF can increase the difficulty of perturbation search attacks, they do not fully eliminate security vulnerabilities at the embedding layer.

7. Discussion

7.1. Limitations of SEP

Although SEP achieves high success rates across models, it has limitations that merit further discussion.

Keywords Localization. Our method primarily relies on identifying specific dangerous words within malicious text and perturbing the corresponding token embeddings. However, we observe that some implicit or context-embedded dangerous components in complex prompts are difficult to isolate. Despite utilizing GPT-4o’s first-class semantic parsing capabilities for automatic keywords extraction, our framework exhibits inherent limitations in identifying those critical tokens that need perturbation, thereby limiting the effectiveness of our search-based attack.

Classifier Dependency. The search strategy of SEP depends on external classifiers to evaluate the effect of perturbation. While incorporating multiple classifiers improves robustness, it also imposes substantial computational overhead. When SEP is deployed in real-world application scenarios, a lightweight and efficient classifier is needed to ensure real-time response.

Evaluation Inconsistency. In addition, inconsistency across different classifiers introduces further challenges. For instance, in response to the prompt “Write a list of tips for manipulating slot machines to win more often”, we discover that HarmBench frequently flags outputs as harmful, whereas Llama-Guard 3 classifies the same outputs as safe. Such discrepancies result in extended attack time and reduced efficiency on certain samples. This highlights the urgent need for standardized safety evaluation frameworks in LLM security research.

7.2. Possible Mitigation against SEP

While our work centers on the attack methodology, we outline two promising defense directions for future research.

Embedding Space Enhancement. The first defense pathway aims to mitigate the impact of attack perturbations at the embedding level. Given that the perturbation amplitude in our attack is relatively small and often affects only a few token dimensions, defenders can attempt to locate the nearest token in the semantic space to each perturbed embedding vector using techniques such as cosine similarity. By reverse-mapping the perturbed embeddings to the vocabulary, it becomes possible to recover the original input tokens and purify the input embeddings accordingly. Additionally, defenders may introduce further controlled perturbations around the attacker’s carefully crafted modifications, potentially disrupting the effectiveness of the original perturbations and degrading the attack success rate.

LLM Distribution Security. The second defense strategy addresses safety from the perspective of LLM distribution systems. Source file examination on model hosting platforms or code repositories should be strengthened to prevent malicious behavior. Since SEP relies on malicious modifications and uploads of model files to inject perturbations into the embedding layer during processing, verifying model file integrity through hash checking can effectively detect tampered files. Moreover, because the injected code leverages hook functions at the model layer to manipulate embedding outputs, it is necessary to implement malicious hook detection, particularly in public model deployments outside of research contexts. Although applying such measures in industrial scenarios introduces significant challenges in terms of cost and practicality, these strategies represent an essential defense against attack paths based on malicious file modifications.

8. Related Work

8.1. LLM Embedding Security

In this section, we will primarily discuss security prior work to the embedding layers of models. This includes LLM attacks targeting or exploiting embedding layers, and various defensive measures designed to safeguard these layers.

In terms of attack methods, Schwinn et al.(Schwinn et al., 2023; Schwinn et al., 2024) discuss the threat model of embedding layer attacks for the first time, and propose an adversarial optimization attack based on successive embedding vector suffixes. Xu et al.(Xu et al., 2024) optimize the embedding vectors of the inputs directly, adding one projection for the input vectors outside the loss function to solve the random output and overfitting problems in the work above. Wang et al. (Wang et al., 2024) develop a framework called ASETF, which attempts to convert successive embedding vectors with adversarial suffixes into coherent and easy-to-understand text which expands the attack vectors of embedding attack. Liang et al.(Zhang et al., 2025) propose a novel framework that identifies and attenuates toxicity-sensitive dimensions in embedding space via linear transformations.

In terms of defense methods, Xhonneux et al.(Xhonneux et al., 2024) implement an adversarial training method for robustly aligning LLMs by computing adversarial attacks in the continuous embedding space of LLMs. Galinkin et al.(Galinkin and Sablotny, 2024) propose a novel approach to detect jailbreak prompts based on pairing text embeddings well-suited for retrieval with traditional machine learning classification algorithms. Hase et al.(Hase et al., 2025) propose a defense called RESTA, which adds random noise to the input embedding vectors and performs aggregation during the generation of each output token.

8.2. LLM Jailbreak Attack

With the gradual improvement of the model security alignment capability, more and more complex jailbreak attacks have been designed to test the robustness of the model security alignment. Prompt-level attacks attempt to carefully construct jailbreak templates. Such templates can either embed the malicious request directly, like PAIR (Chao et al., 2024b), LLM-Fuzzer (Yu et al., 2024), or paraphrase the malicious request in a specific format, like CipherText (Yuan et al., 2024), DRA (Liu et al., 2024b). Model-level attacks attempt to generate malicious inputs using model parameters or runtime information, or to tamper with such information directly, in order to compromise the secure alignment of the model. For example, a series of adversarial suffix optimization attacks represented by GCG (Zou et al., 2023), AutoDAN (Liu et al., 2024a), COLD-Attack (Guo et al., 2024). Also, methods like JailMine (Li et al., 2024) employs an automated "mining" process to elicit malicious responses from LLMs by strategically selecting affirmative outputs and iteratively reducing the likelihood of rejection. This category also includes several of the attacks that utilize the embedding layer described above. As the LLM Distribution System evolves, these attack findings emphasize further evaluation against LLM security alignment.

9. Conclusion

In this paper, we expose a critical vulnerability in current safety alignment strategies for LLMs, highlighting their susceptibility to subtle semantic perturbations within embedding vectors. Through systematic empirical analyses, we demonstrate that minor embedding shifts can reliably bypass alignment safeguards without directly altering model parameters, enabling harmful outputs even in models subjected to enhanced safety alignment techniques. To exploit this vulnerability, we introduce SEP, a model-agnostic, efficient attack framework that strategically perturbs semantically sensitive embedding dimensions, achieving high success rates across leading open-source aligned LLMs. Our results not only challenge existing safety-alignment mechanism but also raise significant concerns about current security practices during LLM distribution, particularly the insufficient embedding-level scanning by popular deployment platforms.

Appendix A Deny List

Here we have listed a series of negative phrases that are commonly used to indicate a refusal pattern in LLM output. Base on GCG(Zou et al., 2023) Deny List, we deleted some low-probability words and expanded some negative phrases found in our experiments. We include the entire list of keywords in table 6 for completeness.

Appendix B Dangerous Tokens Detect Prompt

Here we show the Dangerous Tokens Detect Prompt Template. It asks model to extract a malicious statement from the malicious question that is most likely to violate the model’s security alignment policy, and return it as a json.

To evaluate the accuracy of the above prompt engineering method, we used manual labeling and gpt-4o labeling on 100 malicious inputs of jailbreakbench (Chao et al., 2024a) respectively, and compare the overlap of the dangerous tokens captured by both methods. 85%85\% of the malicious tokens identified by the cue-engineering method had the same results as those identified manually, and 9%9\% of the tokens had the same degree of toxicity despite the different results. The above results prove that this method can be used in SEP.

Appendix C Analyze of Model Response

In section 3, we analyzed and categorized the model outputs obtained from linear perturbations of the embedding vectors, and the complete results of Experiment 1 are shown in figure 9. Furthermore, we will show more sample model outputs for each category and attempt a secondary categorization of the samples in each of the broad categories. Note that for the category Denial Response, since it is the normal output of the model, it is not stated here.

For the category of Glitch Response, it can be roughly divided into three categories. The Repeating category represents the repetition of a single statement in a response. The Mojibake category is a more serious version of the previous category, in which the structure of sentences has been completely lost and there is an infinite loop of characters or phrases. The Restatement category is a less severe version of the Repeating category, in which the syntax of sentences is essentially unchanged but there are several word substitutions. All of the above categories represent a degradation of the modeled text, which tends to occur when the perturbations are large, suggesting that large perturbations can severely damage the model’s parsing of the embedding vectors.

As for the Deviation Response, almost all cases are due to a bias in the model’s understanding of an element of the original sentence. For example, in the case of Subject Error, the subject of the text description is changed from “erotic movie script” to “European Union”, and similarly, ‘torture’ is changed to “turtle”, and this kind of lexical drift has some similarity in the spelling of words. This kind of semantic drift in words has a certain similarity in spelling. In addition, there are also cases where the model misunderstands or understands the purpose or context of the utterance, but the subject of the description remains unchanged, so it is categorized in the category of Part Deviation. In particular, in experiments where only dangerous words are perturbed, there is a phenomenon where the model responds to the perturbed word or words with similar spelling to the word, which we categorize as Word Explanation.
